before.description: Key melody terms and articulation markings you need for the Eduqas listening exam.
before.content_html:
What Is Melody?

Melody is one of the most important musical elements you will need to identify and describe in the Eduqas listening exam. It refers to the main tune or vocal line of a piece of music — the part you would hum or sing along to. To score well, you need precise vocabulary for describing how a melody moves, what shapes it creates, and how individual notes within it are played or sung.

How Melodies Move: Conjunct and Disjunct Motion

Melodies move in two basic ways. Conjunct motion means the melody moves by step — each note is next to the previous one in the scale. This creates a smooth, flowing sound. Disjunct motion means the melody moves by leap — notes jump over one or more scale degrees. This creates a more angular, dramatic sound.

Most melodies use a mixture of both. For example, in Toto’s Africa (a set work for AoS4), the verse melody is described as “mostly conjunct” because it moves mainly in step, with a syncopated rhythm and a syllabic vocal style. However, in Verse 2 (bar 33), the singer leaps up to higher pitches on the words “deep in,” creating a moment of disjunct motion for expressive effect.

Key Fact

Conjunct = stepwise (smooth). Disjunct = leaps (angular). In the exam, always state which type of movement you hear and try to give a bar number or lyric reference as evidence.

Melodic Shape and Contour

As well as describing how a melody moves note-to-note, you should describe its overall shape. A melody might be ascending (going up), descending (going down), or arch-shaped (rising then falling). Some melodies use a narrow pitch range, staying within a few notes, while others have a wide pitch range, spanning many notes.

In Africa, the chorus melody uses only two pitches — the tonic and the leading note — giving it a very narrow pitch range. By contrast, the overall pitch range of the vocal line across the whole song is just under two octaves on the printed score (and even wider on the recording due to vocal improvisations towards the end).

You may be asked to identify which scale a melody is based on. Key scales to know include:

Major scale — bright, happy sound with seven notes. Minor scale — darker, sadder sound with seven notes. Pentatonic scale — a five-note scale that sounds open and folk-like. Chromatic scale — uses all twelve semitones, creating tension or unease.

In the instrumental section of Africa (bars 66–69), the melody uses a B major pentatonic scale with notes falling into groups of three and ending with a triplet. The second half (bars 70–74) switches to the E major scale for more rhythmic variety.

Melodic Decoration: Ornaments

Composers and performers often add decorative notes to a melody. These are called ornaments. The most common ornaments you need to recognise are:

Trill — a rapid alternation between two adjacent notes. Mordent — a quick alternation with the note above or below. Grace notes — small extra notes played quickly before the main note. Turn — a group of notes that “turn” around the main note (above, main, below, main).

In Africa, grace notes and syncopation appear in the instrumental section (bars 75–77), giving the melody a more “pop” style feel.

Key Fact

Grace notes are not essential to the melody or the harmony — they are decorative additions. In the exam, if you hear quick, small notes before a main note, identify them as grace notes or ornaments.

Other Useful Melody Terms

Here are further terms you should use when describing melody in the exam:

Syllabic — one note per syllable of text. Melisma — one syllable sung across several notes (also called melismatic). Riff — a short repeated melodic phrase, common in pop and rock music. Ostinato — a repeated melodic or rhythmic pattern. Sequence — a melodic phrase repeated at a higher or lower pitch. Improvisation — making up a melody on the spot.

In the verse of Africa, the vocal melody is mostly syllabic. However, at the end of Chorus 3, a riff is heard and the melody ends with a melisma. Solo vocal improvisation also appears during the repeated Phrase 3 of Chorus 3.

The verse melody in Africa is a good example to revise for conjunct motion. It is fairly low in the voice, moves conjunctly (by step) in a syncopated rhythm, and is mostly syllabic. Each of the first three phrases falls into two vocal lines of three and five bars respectively, ending with a silent bar. The nine-bar phrase length is unusual and created because Riff A begins as the vocal line ends in bar 8 each time.

In the final eight-bar phrase (bar 32 onwards), the melody begins an octave higher than previously stated and is harmonised by a backing vocalist moving in parallel motion at an interval of a 3rd below. This shift in register adds contrast and builds towards the chorus.

What Is Articulation?

Articulation describes how notes are played or sung. Two performers can play the same notes but make them sound completely different depending on articulation. You must be able to identify and name these techniques in the listening exam.

Key Articulation Markings

These are the main articulation terms the Eduqas spec expects you to know:

Legato — smooth and connected. Notes flow into one another with no gaps. Often shown by a curved line (slur) above or below the notes.

Staccato — short and detached. Each note is separated by a tiny silence. Shown by a dot above or below the note head.

Accent — a note played louder or with more force than the notes around it. Shown by a > symbol. Tenuto — a note held for its full length (or slightly longer), given weight. Shown by a short horizontal line above or below the note.

Slur — a curved line connecting two or more different-pitched notes, indicating they should be played legato. Tie — a curved line connecting two notes of the same pitch, combining their durations. Don’t confuse the two! Pizzicato — plucking string instruments instead of bowing. Arco — returning to bowing after pizzicato. Tremolo — rapid repetition of a single note or rapid alternation between two notes.

Key Fact

A slur connects notes of different pitches (play legato). A tie connects notes of the same pitch (hold the note longer). This is a common point of confusion in exams.

Putting It All Together: Describing Melody and Articulation in the Exam

When you hear a listening extract, work through a mental checklist: Is the melody conjunct or disjunct? What is the pitch range (narrow or wide)? Is it ascending, descending, or arch-shaped? Are there any ornaments such as trills or grace notes? Is the vocal line syllabic or melismatic? What articulation can you hear — legato, staccato, accents? Always try to link your observations to specific moments in the music, using bar numbers or section names where possible.
before.exam_tip_html: In the Eduqas listening exam, the command word “describe” means you need to say what is happening in the music and where. For melody questions, don’t just say “the melody goes up” — use precise terms like “ascending conjunct movement” or “a disjunct leap of a 5th.” For articulation, name the specific technique (e.g. staccato, legato) and say what effect it creates. Always reference bar numbers or section names to show exactly where the feature occurs.

practice_questions.text: Identify the type of melodic movement heard when a melody moves by step.
practice_questions.type: 1 mark — Identification (bar number, instrument, key etc.)

practice_questions.text: State two differences between legato and staccato articulation.
practice_questions.type: 1 mark — Multiple Choice / One-word Answer

1 marks for each valid difference (up to 2 marks):
• Legato is smooth/connected; staccato is short/detached (1)
• Legato is shown by a slur; staccato is shown by a dot (1)
• In legato notes flow into each other; in staccato there are gaps/silences between notes (1)

practice_questions.text: Describe the melodic features of the verse in Toto's Africa.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Short Feature Identification (give bar numbers or identify features)

1 marks for each valid point (up to 4 marks):
• The melody is mostly conjunct / moves by step (1)
• It is fairly low in the voice (1)
• It uses a syncopated rhythm (1)
• It is mostly syllabic (1)
• Nine-bar phrase length is unusual (1)
• Each phrase falls into vocal lines of three and five bars ending with a silent bar (1)

practice_questions.text: Explain how melody is used differently in the verse and the chorus of Toto's Africa.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Short Feature Identification (give bar numbers or identify features)
practice_questions.marks:
1 marks for each valid point (up to 4 marks):
• The verse melody is mostly conjunct; the chorus uses only two pitches (tonic and leading note) (1)
• The verse is fairly low in the voice; the chorus is high in the voice (1)
• The verse melody is syllabic throughout; the chorus melody ends with a melisma (1)
• The verse uses nine-bar phrases (unusual length); the chorus uses four-bar phrases (more regular) (1)
• Vocal improvisation appears in Chorus 3 but not in the verses (1)
• Both verse and chorus use syncopated rhythms (1)

practice_questions.text: Explain how melody and articulation work together to create contrast between a legato vocal line and a staccato accompaniment. Refer to the effect this creates for the listener.
practice_questions.type: 10 marks — Extended Listening Response (explain how music describes/creates effect)
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content (band marks):
Top band (7–10) Detailed, well-structured response using correct terminology. Points may include:
• A legato vocal melody creates a smooth, lyrical quality that draws the listener's attention to the tune
• A staccato accompaniment provides rhythmic energy and lightness underneath
• The contrast between the two articulations creates textural interest
• The listener perceives the melody as the foreground and the accompaniment as background
• This combination is common in classical and pop music
Mid band (4–6) Some correct terminology, partially developed points.
Lower band (1–3) Basic observations with limited terminology.

practice_questions.text: Discuss how a composer might use different types of melodic movement, ornaments, and articulation to create an expressive and varied melody. In your answer, refer to specific techniques and the effects they create.
practice_questions.type: 12 marks — Prepared Extract with Score (multiple sub-questions)
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content (level-based marking, QWC assessed):
Top band (10–12) Thorough and well-organised discussion with accurate terminology throughout. Points may include:
• Conjunct motion creates smooth, lyrical passages; disjunct leaps add drama and interest
• A mix of both prevents the melody from sounding monotonous
• Ornaments such as grace notes, trills, and turns add decoration and character
• Legato articulation sustains a singing quality; staccato adds energy or lightness
• Accents can emphasise important notes or syncopated rhythms
• A melisma at a climactic point adds emotional intensity
• Varying the pitch range (narrow vs wide) creates contrast between sections
• Use of pentatonic or chromatic scales changes the character of the melody
Upper-mid band (7–9) Good range of points with mostly accurate terminology.
Lower-mid band (4–6) Some valid points but limited terminology or development.
Lower band (1–3) Basic points with little use of musical vocabulary.

before.content_html:
Why Dynamics, Tempo and Rhythm Matter

In the Eduqas GCSE Music listening exam, you will need to identify and describe how dynamics, tempo and rhythm are used in both the set work and unfamiliar extracts. Use the correct Italian terminology — not just “loud” or “fast”. This lesson covers every term you need and shows you how they appear in real music.

Dynamics — Italian Terms You Must Know

Dynamics describe how loud or quiet the music is. Composers use Italian terms to indicate dynamics in a score. You need to know the standard range from very quiet to very loud, plus the terms for gradual changes.

Key Fact

The standard dynamic markings from quietest to loudest are: pp (pianissimo — very quiet), p (piano — quiet), mp (mezzo-piano — moderately quiet), mf (mezzo-forte — moderately loud), f (forte — loud), ff (fortissimo — very loud).

Two important terms describe gradual changes in dynamics:

  • Crescendo — getting gradually louder.
  • Diminuendo (also called decrescendo) — getting gradually quieter.

In Baroque music (c.1600–1750), dynamics tend to change suddenly between loud and quiet sections. This is called terraced dynamics. In Romantic music (c.1820–1900), composers used a much wider range of dynamics with gradual crescendos and diminuendos for emotional expression. In the Eduqas set work Africa by Toto, most of the song is at mezzo-forte (mf), whilst the choruses are forte (f) — a clear contrast between sections.

Tempo — Italian Terms for Speed

Tempo tells us how fast or slow the music is. In the exam, you may be asked to give a suitable Italian term for the tempo of an extract. Here are the main terms, from slowest to fastest:

Very Slow

Largo / Lento

A very slow, broad tempo. Often used for solemn or sad music.

Slow

Adagio

Slow and expressive. Common in ballads and gentle pieces.

Walking Pace

Andante

A moderate, walking pace. Neither fast nor slow.

Moderate

Moderato

A medium tempo. Toto’s Africa is described as “moderately fast”.

Fast

Allegro

Fast and lively. Common in upbeat movements and pop songs.

Very Fast

Presto / Vivace

Very fast. Creates energy and excitement.

You also need to know these terms for changes in tempo:

  • Accelerando — gradually getting faster.
  • Rallentando (or ritardando) — gradually getting slower.
  • Rubato — slightly speeding up or slowing down for emotional effect. This is a feature of Romantic-era music.
Key Fact

In the Eduqas listening exam, if you are asked for an Italian term for the tempo, don’t just write “fast” or “slow”. Use terms like Allegro, Adagio, Lento or Andante. In an exam question on the musical Blood Brothers, the accepted answers for a slow tempo were Adagio, Lento or Largo.

Rhythm — Note Values and Rhythmic Devices

Rhythm is the pattern of long and short sounds in music. You need to know the standard note values and how they relate to each other:

  • Semibreve — 4 beats
  • Minim — 2 beats
  • Crotchet — 1 beat
  • Quaver — half a beat
  • Semiquaver — quarter of a beat

Here are the key rhythmic devices the exam may test:

  • Ostinato — a short pattern that repeats over and over. In Africa by Toto, ostinato rhythms consisting almost totally of quavers run throughout the song.
  • Syncopation — placing the emphasis on off-beats or weak beats rather than the strong beats. Africa uses constant syncopation, especially in Riff A.
  • Dotted rhythms — a dot after a note adds half its value again. Dotted rhythms give a lilting or swinging feel. Hedwig’s Theme by John Williams uses dotted rhythms in 3/8 time.
  • Anacrusis — a note or notes that come before the first full bar (a “pick-up”). In Africa, Riff B begins with an anacrusis in bar 3.

Both riffs in the introduction of Africa have their origins in traditional African music through their use of syncopation, the pentatonic scale and irregular ostinato groupings that cut across the 2/2 time signature. Riff A (bars 1–2) is a distinctive syncopated rhythm pattern, while Riff B (bars 3–4) uses an ostinato pattern of five notes. These groupings create a rhythmic tension because they do not line up neatly with the bar lines.

Metre — Time Signatures Explained

Metre is the pattern of strong and weak beats in music. It is shown by the time signature at the start of a piece. You need to recognise the most common time signatures:

  • 4/4 (common time) — four crotchet beats per bar. The most common time signature in popular music.
  • 3/4 — three crotchet beats per bar. Creates a waltz feel.
  • 2/4 — two crotchet beats per bar. Common in marches.
  • 6/8 — six quaver beats per bar, usually grouped in two groups of three. Creates a lilting, swaying feel.
  • 2/2 (split common time or alla breve) — two minim beats per bar. This is the time signature of Africa by Toto throughout the entire song.
  • 3/8 — three quaver beats per bar. Used in Hedwig’s Theme by John Williams, giving it a waltz-like, buoyant feel.
Key Fact

The top number of a time signature tells you how many beats are in each bar. The bottom number tells you the type of beat (4 = crotchet, 8 = quaver, 2 = minim). For example, 6/8 means six quaver beats per bar.

Simple time means each beat divides into two equal parts (e.g. 2/4, 3/4, 4/4). Compound time means each beat divides into three equal parts (e.g. 6/8, 9/8, 12/8). In 6/8, there are two main beats per bar, but each beat is made up of three quavers. Recognising the difference is important — 3/4 and 6/8 both have six quavers per bar, but the grouping and feel are different. In 3/4 the stress is 1-2-3, while in 6/8 the stress is 1-2-3-4-5-6 with two main pulses.

Applying These Elements in the Listening Exam

When you hear an extract in the exam, always listen for dynamics, tempo and rhythm early on. Ask yourself these questions as the music plays:

  • Dynamics: Is it loud or quiet? Does the volume change gradually (crescendo/diminuendo) or suddenly (terraced dynamics)?
  • Tempo: What Italian term best describes the speed? Does the tempo change (accelerando/rallentando)?
  • Rhythm: Can you hear syncopation, ostinatos, dotted rhythms or an anacrusis? What note values are most common?
  • Metre: How many beats can you count per bar? Does it feel like 2, 3 or 4? Is it simple or compound time?

Always use the correct Italian terms in your answers. Credit goes to precise musical vocabulary. For example, writing “the music uses a crescendo from mezzo-forte to fortissimo” is far more effective than “it gets louder”.

The pattern of long and short sounds and silences in music.

_____ composers used a much wider range of dynamics with gradual crescendos and diminuendos for emotional expression

practice_questions.text: You will hear an extract of music four times. Explain how the composer uses dynamics, tempo and rhythm to create mood and atmosphere in this extract. You should refer to specific musical features in your answer.
practice_questions.type: 10 marks — Extended Listening Response (explain how music describes/creates effect)
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content (award up to 10 marks using level descriptors):
Dynamics:
• Identification of dynamic level (e.g. piano, forte, mezzo-forte)
• Identification of dynamic changes (crescendo, diminuendo, sudden contrasts/terraced dynamics)
• Link to mood/atmosphere (e.g. quiet dynamics create calm; crescendo builds tension)
Tempo:
• Appropriate Italian term for the tempo
• Identification of tempo changes (accelerando, rallentando, rubato)
• Link to mood/atmosphere
Rhythm:
• Identification of note values (quavers, semiquavers, dotted rhythms)
• Identification of rhythmic devices (syncopation, ostinato, anacrusis)
• Identification of time signature/metre
• Link to mood/atmosphere

Level descriptors:
9–10: Perceptive answer with detailed explanation and critical judgements. Accurate specialist vocabulary.
7–8: Secure answer with competent account and general judgements. Generally accurate vocabulary.
5–6: Inconsistent answer with some identification and some judgements. Some accurate vocabulary.
3–4: Limited answer with elementary detail and few relevant judgements.
1–2: Very limited answer with little detail and insufficient judgements.
0: No valid information.

before.description: Understanding texture types and common musical structures for the Eduqas listening exam.
before.content_html:
What Is Texture in Music?

Texture describes how the different layers of sound in a piece of music relate to each other. Think of it like fabric — some textures are thin with just one thread, while others are thick with many threads woven together. In the Eduqas listening exam, you need to identify textures by ear and use the correct terminology to describe them.

Types of Texture

There are four main texture types you must know for your exam. Each one describes a different relationship between the musical parts.

Key Fact

The four main textures are: monophonic (one line), homophonic (melody and accompaniment), polyphonic (two or more independent melodies at the same time), and unison (everyone playing or singing the same notes).

Monophonic texture is the simplest type. It means a single melodic line is heard on its own, with no harmony or accompaniment. A solo singer performing without any instruments is monophonic. If several people sing the same melody at the same pitch, this is called unison — it is still considered monophonic because there is only one melodic line.

Homophonic texture is the most common texture in popular music. It features one main melody with an accompaniment underneath. For example, a singer performing with a piano playing chords is homophonic. In Toto’s “Africa,” the overall texture is described as homophonic — there is a lead vocal melody supported by synthesiser chords, bass guitar, and drum kit.

Polyphonic texture (also called contrapuntal) occurs when two or more independent melodies are played or sung at the same time. Each line has its own rhythm and shape. A round like “Row, Row, Row Your Boat” is a simple example. In “Africa,” a moment of polyphonic texture occurs in Verse 2, where a countermelody (or descant) on a flute-like instrument is heard across the top of the texture alongside the lead vocal.

In the exam, you may also need to describe how texture changes within a piece. Common descriptions include:

  • Layering — new parts are gradually added to build up the texture (as in the 8-bar percussion intro to “Africa,” where rhythm parts are looped and layered).
  • Thinning — parts are removed to reduce the texture (as in the outro of “Africa,” where the texture is gradually reduced until only the rhythm track and the bass line of Riff A remain).
  • Thickening — more instruments or voices join, making the texture fuller. In “Africa,” the choruses are forte with a full band texture, thicker than the verses.
Key Fact

In the Eduqas listening exam, you may be asked to identify a change in texture at a specific point in the music. Listen for when instruments enter or drop out, and whether the melody has accompaniment (homophonic) or another independent melody (polyphonic).

What Is Structure in Music?

Structure (also called form) refers to how a piece of music is organised into sections. Recognising structure means being able to hear when sections repeat, change, or return. The Eduqas spec requires you to identify and describe common structures in both popular music and classical music.

Common Structures in Popular Music

Most popular songs follow a verse–chorus structure. The verse tells the story with different lyrics each time, while the chorus is the catchy, repeated section. Many songs add a bridge (sometimes called a middle 8) for contrast before the final chorus.

“Africa” by Toto uses a verse–chorus structure. The full layout is:

Intro

Bars 1–4 (repeated)

8-bar unpitched percussion intro followed by Riff A played 4 times. Key of B major. Layered rhythm parts and ostinatos show African influence.

Verse 1

Bars 5–39 (B major)

35 bars. Four phrases: three 9-bar phrases and one 8-bar phrase. The unusual 9-bar length occurs because Riff A begins as the vocal line ends in bar 8 each time.

Chorus 1

18 bars (A major)

Key changes to A major. Four phrases with the chord loop F#m–D–A–E (vi–IV–I–V).

Link 1

8 bars (B major)

Returns to B major. Based on Riff A material, connecting chorus back to verse.

Verse 2

B major

Shortened — only two 9-bar phrases plus the final 8-bar phrase. Features a countermelody on a flute-like instrument and more prominent backing vocals.

Chorus 2 & Link 2

A major / B major

Chorus 2 repeats Chorus 1. Link 2 repeats Link 1.

Instrumental

Bars 66–82 (B major)

Based on verse accompaniment but vocal melody replaced by instrumental melody based on Riff B. Even shorter than Verse 2.

Chorus 3

22 bars (A major)

Longer than previous choruses. “I bless the rains down in Africa” is heard five times. Solo vocal improvisation is added. A new electric guitar riff appears.

Outro

B major

Repeats intro material. Texture gradually reduces — fades out to just the rhythm track and bass line of Riff A.

Other Structures You Need to Know

The Eduqas spec covers several structural forms beyond verse–chorus. You may hear these in any area of study.

Ternary form (ABA) — Three sections where the first section (A) returns after a contrasting middle section (B). The return of A gives the piece a sense of balance. Some composition briefs ask students to write in ternary form.

Rondo form (ABACADA…) — A main theme (A) keeps returning between contrasting episodes (B, C, D, etc.). Each episode introduces new material, but the listener always hears the familiar A section come back.

Theme and variations — A theme is stated and then altered in a series of variations. Each variation changes one or more elements — for example, the melody might be decorated, the rhythm changed, or the key shifted from major to minor.

32-bar song form (AABA) — Common in older pop and jazz. Four 8-bar sections: the A section is heard three times with a contrasting B section (the bridge or middle 8) before the final return of A.

Through-composed — Music that is continuously different with no repeated sections. Each verse or section has new music. This is common in film music where the score follows the action on screen.

In addition to naming overall structures, you should be able to identify these structural devices:

  • Intro — the opening section before the main melody or vocal enters.
  • Outro / Coda — the closing section. In “Africa,” the outro uses a fade out.
  • Ostinato — a short repeated pattern. Riff B in “Africa” uses an ostinato pattern of five notes based on the E major pentatonic scale.
  • Riff — a short repeated phrase, often played on guitar or keyboard. “Africa” features two main riffs (Riff A and Riff B) that recur throughout the song.
  • Link / Transition — a short passage connecting two main sections.
  • Repeat and fade — a section is repeated while the volume gradually decreases to silence, as heard in the outro of “Africa.”

Texture and Structure in “Africa” — Putting It Together

In the exam, you may need to describe how texture and structure work together. In “Africa,” texture changes help define the structure:

  • The intro builds texture through layering — unpitched percussion enters first, then pitched instruments playing Riff A are added.
  • The verses are mostly homophonic with a lead vocal over chordal accompaniment. In Verse 2, the texture becomes more complex as a countermelody and backing vocals are added.
  • The choruses are thicker and louder (forte) with the full band and backing vocals creating a fuller homophonic texture.
  • The outro thins the texture, gradually stripping parts away until only the rhythm track and bass line remain, creating a fade out.
Key Fact

Verse 2 of “Africa” differs from Verse 1 because it adds a countermelody (descant) on a flute-like instrument and more prominent backing vocals harmonising on “Ooo.” This makes the texture more complex — a detail worth naming in your answers.

before.content_html:
What Is Harmony?

Harmony refers to the combination of notes sounding together at the same time. When you hear a chord being played on a piano or guitar, you are hearing harmony. In the Eduqas GCSE Music listening exam, you need to identify chords, describe chord progressions, and explain how harmony creates mood and atmosphere.

Harmony is closely linked to tonality. While harmony is about which chords are used, tonality is about the overall key — whether the music sounds major or minor, and which note feels like “home.”

Primary and Secondary Chords

Every major or minor key has seven chords built on each degree of the scale. These are labelled with Roman numerals. The three most important are the primary chords:

  • Chord I (the tonic) — built on the first note of the scale. This is the “home” chord.
  • Chord IV (the subdominant) — built on the fourth note.
  • Chord V (the dominant) — built on the fifth note.

For example, in the key of G major the primary chords are G (I), C (IV) and D (V). In a major key, all three primary chords are major chords.

Secondary chords are built on the remaining degrees of the scale: ii, iii, vi and vii. In a major key, chords ii, iii and vi are minor, while chord vii is diminished. Pop and rock music often uses chord vi heavily — for example, the chorus of Africa by Toto uses the progression vi–IV–I–V (F#m–D–A–E in A major), which is a very common pop chord pattern.

Key Fact

In a major key, primary chords (I, IV, V) are all major. The most commonly used secondary chords in pop music are ii (minor), iii (minor), and vi (minor). Chord vii is diminished and is rarely used on its own in popular music.

Upper-case Roman numerals (I, IV, V) indicate major chords. Lower-case numerals (ii, iii, vi) indicate minor chords. A small circle after the numeral (vii°) means the chord is diminished. In the exam, you may see either format. For example, in Africa by Toto, the intro chords in B major are written as ♮VII–vi–ii (A–G#m–C#m). The natural sign (♮) before VII tells you the chord has been flattened from what the key signature would normally give.

Chord Progressions in Popular Music

A chord progression is the order in which chords are played. Many pop songs are built on short, repeating chord loops. Here are some of the most common progressions you will hear:

  • I–V–vi–IV — an extremely common “four-chord” pop progression.
  • vi–IV–I–V — the same four chords starting on the minor chord. This is the progression used in the chorus of Africa by Toto (F#m–D–A–E in A major).
  • I–IV–V — the simplest primary-chord-only progression, common in rock and blues.

The rate at which chords change is called the harmonic rhythm. In the verse sections of Africa, the harmonic rhythm is mostly one chord per bar. In the chorus, the same one-chord-per-bar pattern continues. Faster harmonic rhythm (more chord changes per bar) can create excitement or tension; slower harmonic rhythm feels more stable and relaxed.

Key Fact

In the chorus of Africa by Toto, the chord progression vi–IV–I–V (F#m–D–A–E) is a typical pop song chord pattern. The first three phrases of the chorus all use this same four-bar loop before the final phrase changes chords to prepare the key shift back to B major.

Power Chords

In rock music, guitarists often use power chords instead of full major or minor chords. A power chord contains only the root and the fifth — there is no third. Because the third is the note that makes a chord sound major or minor, a power chord is neither. This gives rock music its raw, aggressive sound. Power chords are often played on electric guitar with distortion.

Diatonic and Chromatic Harmony

Diatonic harmony means the chords use only the notes that belong to the key. Most popular music is diatonic. The background notes for Africa by Toto describe the harmony as “diatonic throughout,” meaning the chords stay within the notes of the key in each section.

Chromatic harmony uses notes from outside the key. This can sound surprising, mysterious, or tense. In film music, composers like John Williams use chromatic harmony to create an otherworldly atmosphere — for example, Hedwig’s Theme uses “unusual, non-functional chromatic chords” to create a sense of magic.

A chord is in inversion when a note other than the root is placed in the bass (the lowest sounding note). In Africa, the verse uses several inversions such as B/F# (chord I with the fifth in the bass, written as Ic) and A/E (♮VII with the fifth in the bass, written as ♮VIIc). Inversions create smoother bass lines and more interesting movement between chords.

Tonality — Major and Minor Keys

Tonality describes the key of a piece — whether it sounds bright and happy (major) or dark and sad (minor). You need to be able to identify tonality by ear in the listening exam.

  • Major — sounds bright, positive, confident. Example: the chorus of Africa is in A major.
  • Minor — sounds dark, sad, mysterious. Often used in horror film music to build tension.

Some pieces change key during the music. This is called modulation. In Africa by Toto, the majority of the song is in B major, but the choruses all shift to A major. This modulation gives the chorus a different, brighter feel compared to the verses.

Intro/Links (B major): Three chords only — ♮VII (A), vi (G#m) and ii (C#m). These are presented in two riffs, each lasting two bars. Riff a uses a syncopated rhythm pattern; Riff b uses a pentatonic ostinato over a sustained chord ii.

Verses (B major): A longer 9-bar chord sequence: I–iii–vi–Ic–♮VIIc–IV–vi–♮VII–vi–ii (B–D#m7–G#m7–B/F#–A/E–E/F#–G#m7–A–G#m7–C#m). This repeats with variations. Note the use of chord inversions (B/F#, A/E, E/F#) to create a smooth bass line.

Choruses (A major): A typical pop chord pattern — vi–IV–I–V (F#m–D–A–E). The final phrase alters to vi–IV–I–iii–V–vi to prepare the shift back to B major for the next section.

Cadences

A cadence is a pair of chords that marks the end of a musical phrase. Cadences function like punctuation in language — they tell the listener whether a musical sentence has finished, paused, or been interrupted. You must be able to identify four types of cadence by ear for the listening exam.

Perfect cadence (V → I): This is the strongest ending in music. It moves from the dominant chord to the tonic chord, creating a powerful sense of resolution and finality. Think of it as a full stop. Almost every piece of tonal music ends with a perfect cadence.

Imperfect cadence (any chord → V): This cadence ends on the dominant chord, which sounds unfinished and questioning — like a comma in a sentence. It creates the expectation that more music will follow. Any chord can lead into an imperfect cadence, but the most common progressions are I → V and ii → V.

Plagal cadence (IV → I): Sometimes called the “Amen” cadence because it is the progression heard at the end of many hymns when the congregation sings “Amen.” It moves from the subdominant to the tonic and sounds gentle, warm, and complete — but less dramatic than a perfect cadence.

Interrupted cadence (V → vi): This is the surprise cadence. The listener expects chord V to resolve to chord I (as in a perfect cadence), but instead it moves to chord vi (the relative minor). The effect is unexpected and can sound poignant, dramatic, or even humorous depending on the context.

Key Fact

Perfect (V → I) = finished, like a full stop. Imperfect (any → V) = unfinished, like a comma. Plagal (IV → I) = gentle ending, the “Amen” cadence. Interrupted (V → vi) = surprise, the unexpected twist. In the exam, listen for phrase endings and ask: does it sound finished (perfect or plagal), unfinished (imperfect), or surprising (interrupted)?

Listen for the moments where a musical phrase feels like it reaches a resting point. Then ask yourself: does the phrase sound finished (like the end of a sentence) or unfinished (like a pause before continuing)? If it sounds finished and strong, it is likely a perfect cadence (V → I). If it sounds finished but softer and more gentle, it could be a plagal cadence (IV → I). If it sounds unfinished and you feel the music wants to continue, it is probably an imperfect cadence (ending on V). If it sounds like a surprise — you expected the phrase to end but it took an unexpected turn — it is likely an interrupted cadence (V → vi).

Modulation in Detail

You already know that modulation means changing key during a piece. Now let’s look at the two most common types of modulation you need to recognise in the exam.

Modulation to the dominant: This means moving from the home key to the key built on the fifth note of the scale. For example, from C major to G major, or from D major to A major. This is the most common modulation in Western music. It creates a brighter, more energised feel because the new key is closely related to the original. In sonata form and binary form, music often modulates to the dominant in the first section.

Modulation to the relative minor: This means moving from a major key to its relative minor — the minor key that shares the same key signature. For example, from C major to A minor, or from G major to E minor. This modulation creates a darker, more melancholic mood while remaining harmonically close to the original key.

How do you spot a modulation? Listen for three clues: (1) new accidentals — sharps or flats that were not in the original key, (2) a new tonal centre — a different note now feels like “home,” and (3) cadences in the new key — if you hear a perfect cadence (V → I) and the “I” chord is in a different key from where the piece started, a modulation has occurred.

Key Fact

The two most common modulations: (1) to the dominant (e.g. C major → G major) — sounds brighter; (2) to the relative minor (e.g. C major → A minor) — sounds darker. Spot modulation by listening for new accidentals, a shift in tonal centre, and cadences in the new key.

Other Tonality Terms You Need to Know

The exam may test you on several related tonality terms beyond major and minor:

  • Atonal — music with no sense of key at all. It sounds unsettled and is often used in horror film scores.
  • Modal — music based on modes (scales from medieval music) rather than standard major or minor scales. Modal music has a distinctive, sometimes ancient-sounding quality.
  • Pentatonic — based on a five-note scale. In Africa, Riff b in the intro uses the E major pentatonic scale. Pentatonic melodies and harmonies are common in African, Chinese, and folk music traditions.
Key Fact

In Africa by Toto, the tonality shifts between B major (verses, intro, links, instrumental, outro) and A major (all three choruses). The harmony is described as diatonic throughout, meaning all chords stay within the notes of whichever key the section is in.

before.content_html:
What Are Instrumentation and Timbre?

In the Eduqas GCSE Music listening exam, you will be asked to identify instruments and describe the quality of the sounds they make. These two skills fall under two spec headings: instrumentation and timbre (also called sonority). Instrumentation is about which instruments are playing. Timbre is about how those instruments sound — bright, warm, harsh, mellow, breathy, and so on.

Being able to name an instrument is only part of the job. The exam rewards you for describing what makes that instrument’s sound distinctive and how it contributes to the overall effect of the music.

Key Fact

Timbre and sonority mean the same thing on this exam. Both refer to the tone colour or quality of a sound. Use whichever term you prefer, but make sure you can describe sounds with precise adjectives (e.g. “bright,” “mellow,” “piercing,” “warm”).

The Four Orchestral Instrument Families

Orchestral instruments are grouped into four families based on how they produce sound. You must be able to place any standard orchestral instrument into the correct family.

The string family produces sound by vibrating strings, either with a bow or by plucking. Instruments include violin, viola, cello, double bass, and harp. Common articulations include arco (bowed), pizzicato (plucked), double stopping (two strings at once), and tremolo (rapid repetition of a note). Timbre descriptions: warm, rich, lyrical, resonant, thin (high violin), dark and sonorous (cello).

Woodwind instruments produce sound by blowing air across a mouthpiece or through a reed. Key instruments: flute, oboe, clarinet, bassoon, and piccolo. The flute has a bright, breathy, silvery timbre. The oboe sounds nasal and piercing. The clarinet can be warm and mellow in its low register or bright and clear higher up. The bassoon has a deep, reedy, sometimes humorous tone.

Brass instruments produce sound by the player buzzing their lips into a cup-shaped mouthpiece. Key instruments: trumpet, French horn, trombone, and tuba. Brass can sound bold, powerful, majestic, or heroic when loud. When played softly or with a mute (con sordino), the timbre becomes muffled, distant, or haunting.

Percussion instruments are struck, shaken, or scraped. They split into two groups: pitched percussion (e.g. xylophone, marimba, timpani, glockenspiel) and unpitched percussion (e.g. snare drum, bass drum, cymbals, tambourine). Timbres range from sharp and metallic (triangle, glockenspiel) to deep and booming (bass drum, timpani) or dry and rattling (snare drum).

Acoustic vs Electronic Instruments

In popular music, you will hear a mixture of acoustic and electronic instruments. You must be able to sort common instruments into these two categories.

Acoustic instruments: vocals, piano, acoustic guitar, drum kit, strings (violin, cello etc.), horn section, and standard percussion. Electronic instruments: keyboard, electric guitar, bass guitar, synthesiser, drum machine, and sampler.

Some instruments can be either acoustic or electronic depending on how they are used. For example, an electric guitar is electronic because it relies on amplification, whereas an acoustic guitar produces sound from its hollow body alone.

Key Fact

In Toto’s “Africa” (the Eduqas set work), the instrumentation includes drum kit, additional unpitched percussion, lead electric guitar, bass guitar, synthesiser, male lead vocals, and male backing vocals. The instrumental sonorities used — including xylophones and marimbas — suggest the sounds of pitched percussion instruments originating from the African continent.

Instruments in Rock and Pop Music

Rock music typically uses electric and bass guitars, a drum kit, and vocals. The electric guitar often uses effects such as distortion to create a gritty, aggressive timbre. The drum kit keeps the momentum pushing forward with driving rhythms and brings intensity.

In recorded rock and pop music, panning is used most commonly on the drum kit. It can also be used on electric guitars (especially if there are multiple guitar parts) and backing vocals, spreading the instruments across the stereo field.

Rock bands often have a lead singer, with other members providing backing vocals. It is common for rock singers to use falsetto to bring intensity. Pop music uses a broader range of instruments, frequently combining acoustic sounds (piano, strings, horn section) with electronic sounds (keyboard, synthesiser, drum machine).

Music Technology and Timbre

Music technology plays a huge role in shaping timbre in modern music. You should know the following key tools and effects:

Synthesisers use oscillators to produce a wide range of electronic sounds, from pads and leads to imitations of acoustic instruments. Samplers trigger pre-recorded sounds — drums and percussion are the most commonly sampled sounds.

Effects change the timbre of a sound after it has been produced. Reverb makes a sound seem as if it is in a different space — a sports hall, a cave, a bathroom. Phasing creates a swirling or whooshing sound by playing two identical signals slightly out of sync.

A DAW (Digital Audio Workstation) is the software used to produce music. Examples include Logic, Pro Tools, and Ableton. DAWs allow musicians to record, use virtual instruments, add effects plugins, and edit tracks endlessly.

Describing Timbre in the Exam

When describing timbre in your exam answers, always be specific. Avoid vague words like “nice” or “interesting.” Instead, use precise adjectives linked to the instrument and its playing technique. Here are some useful timbre words organised by character:

Bright / Light: shimmering, sparkling, silvery, piercing, crisp. Dark / Heavy: sonorous, deep, thunderous, booming, rich. Smooth: warm, mellow, velvety, lyrical, legato. Rough / Aggressive: harsh, gritty, distorted, raspy, strident. Thin / Airy: breathy, ethereal, delicate, transparent, hollow.

Key Fact

A strong exam answer combines the instrument name, the playing technique or effect, and a timbre description. For example: “The electric guitar uses distortion, creating a harsh, gritty timbre” is far better than “The guitar sounds loud.”

In Toto’s “Africa,” the eight-bar percussion introduction uses only unpitched percussion instruments with layered rhythm parts and ostinatos, giving a dry, rhythmic, African-influenced timbre. The xylophones and marimbas that follow have a bright, resonant, bell-like sonority that suggests traditional African pitched percussion. The vocal melody is fairly low in the voice and mostly syllabic, while the backing vocals in the chorus add a richer, fuller sonority with parallel harmony at a third below.
before.exam_tip_html: In the Eduqas listening exam, identification questions often ask you to name the instrument family (strings, woodwind, brass, percussion) or a specific solo instrument. Always listen for the method of sound production: is it bowed, blown, struck, or electronic? For longer “describe” or “explain” questions about timbre, use the formula: instrument + technique/effect + timbre adjective + impact on the music. For example: “The flute plays a legato melody with a bright, silvery timbre, creating a calm and gentle atmosphere.” Avoid generic words like “nice” or “good” — examiners want precise musical vocabulary.
